design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (Review Manager 5.4.1, inverse variance) of placebo-controlled randomized trials of bupropion, alone or combined with another medication or psychosocial treatment, for amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder diagnosed by DSM-IV or DSM-5; PROSPERO CRD42022362962; searched to 31 October 2022. Eight trials (nine reports, because the two stages of Trivedi et al., 2021, were entered separately); 1239 participants as counted by the review. Main outcome: the proportion of amphetamine-positive urine samples (or positive weeks), pooled as a risk ratio; secondary outcomes retention, adherence, craving, addiction severity, depressive symptoms, dropout after adverse events and serious adverse events.
can_establish: The direction and rough size of the difference between bupropion and placebo in the share of amphetamine-positive urine samples, and in retention, adherence, craving, depression and adverse events, across the trials published to October 2022, with the review's own GRADE ratings.
cannot_establish: A precise effect of bupropion on use (the urine outcome counts each of 15,664 samples as an independent observation, so its intervals are too narrow); any effect on abstinence or on how many people stop using (not analysed); the effect of bupropion alone apart from its combination with naltrexone (about half of the review's participants come from one combination trial); absolute effects (no event rates are given in the article); or effects beyond 12 weeks.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, EBM Reviews, EMBASE, PubMed and Web of Science, six trial registries, Google Scholar and the FDA, Health Canada and EMA websites, plus reference lists, to 31 October 2022; strategies designed by a librarian and peer-reviewed with the PRESS checklist (2.2, p. 2). 2623 records, 2142 screened, 35 sought in full text, 34 assessed, 8 trials included (Figure 1, p. 4). Primary trials: seven in the USA and one in Iran, run between 2003 and 2019 (Table 1, p. 5).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized placebo-controlled trials with a bupropion arm at any dose, with or without another medication (such as naltrexone) or psychosocial treatment, in people with amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder diagnosed by DSM-IV or DSM-5; reports in English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, Arabic, Persian or French. Excluded: open-label, human-laboratory and animal studies, and trials with fewer than five participants per arm (2.3, p. 2).
sample.demographics: Trials of 19 to 403 participants; mean or median ages 17.5 to 42 years (one adolescent pilot, Heinzerling et al., 2013); 42% to 100% men (two trials in men only, Das et al., 2010, and Ghoreishi et al., 2017). Study conditions: bupropion SR 300 mg daily for 8 or 12 weeks in seven trials; 450 mg daily with injectable naltrexone for two 6-week stages in Trivedi et al. (2021). Psychosocial co-interventions are listed for six trials and given as not available for Ghoreishi et al. (2017) and Trivedi et al. (2021) (Table 1, p. 5).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; retention was pooled as an outcome (seven reports, 786 participants).
sample.selection_effects: Two trials contributed no urine data because their results were unavailable after the authors were contacted: Anderson et al. (2015), with 204 participants the largest bupropion-alone trial, and Ghoreishi et al. (2017), with 50 (Table 2, p. 6). The urine outcome therefore rests on five bupropion-alone trials with 357 participants (editors' sum from Table 1) and on the two stages of the naltrexone-plus-bupropion trial (403 people, of whom the 225 placebo non-responders re-randomized in stage 2 are entered again). The authors note that trials excluded many people with physical and mental comorbidity and included few women.

exposure.measurement: Bupropion or placebo as assigned in the primary trials.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in the primary trials: bupropion SR 300 mg daily by mouth for 8 to 12 weeks (seven trials); 450 mg daily by mouth with extended-release injectable naltrexone every 3 weeks for two 6-week stages (Trivedi et al., 2021) (Table 1 and its footnotes, p. 5).
exposure.polysubstance: Not analysed; the authors note that most trials did not report other substance use disorders such as opioid or alcohol use disorder, so the results may not apply to people who use several drugs (4.1, p. 10).

comparison.controls: Placebo in each primary trial, with the same co-interventions as the bupropion arm.
comparison.matching: Randomization within each trial; the review pools within-trial comparisons.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to randomized comparisons; whether participants used amphetamine or methamphetamine was not distinguished across trials (4.1, p. 10).

outcomes.instruments: Urine tests for amphetamine or methamphetamine during the randomized phase (proportion of positive samples; positive weeks in Elkashef et al., 2008; derived from a treatment-effectiveness score, the mean number of negative urine samples, in the two Heinzerling trials); retention to the end of the randomized phase; adherence by pill counts or MEMS caps; craving by visual analogue scale or Brief Substance Craving Scale at week 4 and at end of treatment; Addiction Severity Index sub-scores; depressive symptoms (HAM-D, BDI, PHQ-9); dropout after adverse events; serious adverse events. Self-reported use, withdrawal, anxiety and cognition were planned but dropped for lack of data (2.4, p. 3; Table 2, p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Urine testing is objective; the pooled proportion combines collection once, twice or three times a week, which the review treats as comparable (3.3, p. 4). Primary trials were appraised with RoB 2 (cited as Higgins et al., 2011) in duplicate, and each outcome was rated with GRADE in duplicate (2.6, p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit on use is a lower proportion of amphetamine-positive urine samples (or positive weeks) on bupropion than on placebo, pooled across trials as a risk ratio in which each urine sample counts as one observation (2.4, p. 3; 3.4.1, p. 4; Table 3, p. 7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; P of .05 or less was used for each of 15 pooled estimates (eight outcomes, with addiction severity split into seven sub-scores) and for four sets of subgroup analyses per outcome (2.7, p. 3; Tables 3 and 4).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Title and abstract screening, full-text selection, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment and GRADE were each done independently by two reviewers with consensus (2.3, 2.5, 2.6, pp. 2–3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Urine outcome (7 reports, 15,664 samples): RR 0.90 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.96), P < .001, I² 89%, GRADE very low; excluding the trial at high risk of bias, 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92); excluding Elkashef et al. (positive weeks), 0.91 (0.85 to 0.97). By medication (Table 4): bupropion 300 mg without naltrexone, 5 trials, 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00); 450 mg with naltrexone, the 2 stages of Trivedi et al., 0.92 (0.89 to 0.94); difference between subgroups not significant. By duration: 12-week trials (4) 0.85 (0.78 to 0.93) vs shorter trials (Trivedi's two stages and Heinzerling et al., 2013) 0.98 (0.89 to 1.08), a significant subgroup difference. Less-than-daily use (2 trials) 1.09 (0.56 to 2.11). Retention (7 reports, 786 participants): RR 0.97 (0.89 to 1.05), I² 6%, GRADE high. Adherence (6 reports, 119,680 pills): RR 0.91 (0.84 to 0.99), favouring placebo, I² 99%, GRADE very low. Craving at week 4 (4 reports, 373): SMD 0.04 (−0.16 to 0.24), I² 0%, GRADE moderate; at end of treatment (6 reports, 939): SMD −0.38 (−0.63 to −0.13), I² 64%, all six at high risk of bias, GRADE very low. Depressive symptoms (5 reports, 874): SMD −0.06 (−0.26 to 0.14). Addiction Severity Index legal status (2 reports, 148): SMD −0.47 (−0.83 to −0.11); six other sub-scores not significant. Dropout after adverse events (4 reports, 391): RD 0.03 (−0.01 to 0.07). Serious adverse events (8 reports, 1189): RD −0.01 (−0.02 to 0.01), GRADE low. No tau², prediction intervals or event rates are given in the article.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; subgroup analyses by co-medication with naltrexone and dose, baseline frequency of use, sex and treatment duration, all at study level (2.7.2, p. 3; Table 4, p. 9).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42022362962, registered on 7 October 2022, after a limited scoping search and before the full search (to 31 October 2022); the protocol is Appendix 1 (not read) (2.1, p. 2). Declared deviation: four planned outcomes (self-reported use, withdrawal, anxiety and cognition) dropped for lack of poolable data (2.4, p. 3). Whether the subgroup and sensitivity analyses were planned is not stated in the article.
analysis.selective_reporting: Per-trial risk-of-bias judgments, forest plots, funnel plots, GRADE tables and the list of excluded studies are only in the appendices, which were not read. The largest bupropion-alone trial (Anderson et al., 2015) and Ghoreishi et al. (2017) are absent from the main outcome because their urine data were unavailable (Table 2, p. 6).
analysis.power: Not applicable; several pooled outcomes rest on two to four reports.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across seven reports, the share of amphetamine-positive urine samples was about 10% lower in relative terms on bupropion (RR 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96), with very high heterogeneity (I² 89%) and very low certainty by the review's own GRADE. Each urine sample is treated as an independent observation, so all the urine intervals are too narrow. For bupropion alone (five trials, 357 participants) the estimate is 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00). About half of the review's participants come from one trial that combined bupropion with naltrexone, with 225 of its participants counted twice. Retention did not differ (0.97, 0.89 to 1.05), adherence was lower on bupropion, and no absolute rates are reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Abstract and Conclusion report a significant, modest reduction in use and craving rated as very low-quality evidence, larger in men (craving) and with longer treatment (use); the Conclusion adds that the clinical relevance of such a small effect should be verified, a fair caution, and the Discussion acknowledges that the combination trial may have pulled results towards benefit (pp. 1, 10). But the finding in men rests on one men-only trial at high risk of bias for craving (Ghoreishi et al., 2017) (Discussion, 9th paragraph, p. 10), and the duration finding compares 12-week bupropion-alone trials with the 6-week stages of the naltrexone combination plus one 19-person adolescent pilot, so duration is confounded with medication and population (Table 4, p. 9). The total of 1239 participants counts 225 people twice, and the unit-of-analysis problem behind the urine and adherence intervals is not mentioned.

timeline.event: Bhatt et al.: in a meta-analysis of psychostimulants, bupropion did not increase urine-verified abstinence at the end of treatment (bupropion subgroup OR 1.12, 0.54 to 2.33); this review notes that Bhatt et al. analysed abstinence, not the share of positive samples, and predates the 2021 combination trial.
Siefried et al.: systematic review described by this review as showing possible benefits of bupropion on use that were not statistically significant in the included trials.
Trivedi et al.: two-stage trial of injectable naltrexone plus bupropion, entered here as two reports.
Apuy et al.: meta-analysis of bupropion with cognitive behavioural therapy (five studies), described by this review as finding no overall reduction in recurrence of use (not read).
This review: RR 0.90 (0.84 to 0.96) for the share of positive urine samples across seven reports; 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00) for bupropion alone.

replication.where_it_stands: On the share of positive urine samples, the pooled estimate leans slightly towards bupropion, but the method overstates its precision and much of the estimate comes from the naltrexone combination trial; for bupropion alone the interval reaches no effect. No difference has been shown in end-of-treatment abstinence (Bhatt et al., 2016) or in retention (this review).

funding.funder: Canadian Institutes of Health Research (grant REN-181675), Université de Montréal and the Centre de recherche du Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CRCHUM); the sponsor had no role in conceptualization, data acquisition and analysis, interpretation of results, or drafting and editing (Funding sources/sponsors, pp. 10–11). Individual authors' salary or career awards are listed in the Acknowledgements (p. 11).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed (Declaration of Competing Interest, p. 11): PB is site principal investigator for an upcoming trial of psychostimulants for methamphetamine use disorder; CGS is a consultant at Clearmind Medicine; NE has NHMRC funding for a study of lisdexamfetamine for methamphetamine use disorder; KS has NCCRED funding for a pilot study of lisdexamfetamine for methamphetamine withdrawal; BLF reports funding, in-kind donations, study medication or consultancy from Pfizer, Indivior, Aurora Cannabis, Bioprojet Pharma, Brainsway, Canopy Growth, Alcohol Countermeasure Systems, Alkermes, Universal Ibogaine and Shionogi (printed 'Shinogi'); DJA receives study material from Cardiol Therapeutics and Exka for trials funded by the Quebec Ministry of Health and Social Services. All other authors declare no conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Montréal (CRCHUM, Université de Montréal), Toronto (CAMH and the University of Toronto), Vancouver (BC Centre on Substance Use, UBC) and Sydney (St Vincent's Hospital, NCCRED, NDARC). No review author appears among the authors of the included trials in the reference list; Steven Shoptaw is thanked for providing results from his trial; the reference list shows him as an author of five of the eight trials (Das et al., 2010; Heinzerling et al., 2013 and 2014; Shoptaw et al., 2008; Trivedi et al., 2021), so the trials are not fully independent of one another. Walter Ling is an author of Elkashef et al. (2008), Shoptaw et al. (2008) and Trivedi et al. (2021), and Elkashef et al. (2008) shares eight authors with Anderson et al. (2015) (Elkashef, Anderson, Li, Holmes, Chiang, Kahn, Campbell and Haning); only Ghoreishi et al. (2017), from Iran, shares no author with the others, and it gave no urine data. Every one of the seven urine reports therefore shares at least one author with another (reference list, pp. 11–12). Ezard and Siefried are authors of the 2020 systematic review that this review discusses.

what_would_settle_it: A participant-level meta-analysis of the bupropion-alone trials that analyses urine results within people (allowing for repeated samples) and reports abstinence and use days, or a large independent trial of bupropion alone with a urine-verified primary outcome and follow-up after treatment ends.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (DSM-IV or DSM-5 amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder), intervention (bupropion, alone or combined), comparator (placebo) and outcomes are specified (2.3, 2.4).

PROSPERO CRD42022362962, registered on 7 October 2022 before the full search, with the protocol in Appendix 1 (not read); the dropped outcomes are explained, but whether the subgroup and sensitivity analyses were planned is not stated.

The review states that it focuses on placebo-controlled randomized trials of efficacy and safety, and excludes open-label, laboratory and animal studies and trials with fewer than five per arm to limit small-sample bias; the explanation is brief.

Seven databases, six trial registries, grey literature, regulators' websites and reference lists, librarian-designed and peer-reviewed strategies, search about a year before online publication (31 October 2022; online 4 November 2023) and authors contacted for data; but reports were limited to seven languages without a stated reason (2.3, p. 2). AMSTAR 2 gives partial yes only when publication restrictions such as language are justified, so the item is not met.
Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts independently, with consensus (2.3).
Two reviewers extracted independently, with consensus (2.5).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The article says the excluded full-text reports and the reasons are in Appendix 5, which was not read; Figure 1 gives the reasons with counts (17 duplicate study populations, 1 wrong population, 2 wrong comparator, 4 wrong design, 1 probable duplicate, 1 with fewer than five per group).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives dates, country, size, age, sex, frequency of use, ADHD, medication and dose, duration and co-interventions; setting, recruitment source and whether participants used amphetamine or methamphetamine are not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 applied in duplicate, by outcome, which covers allocation concealment, blinding and selection of the reported result; per-trial judgments are only in Appendix 8 (not read), and the tool is cited with the 2011 paper describing the original Cochrane tool.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Random-effects inverse-variance pooling is appropriate in itself, but the main outcome pools per-arm counts of positive urine samples (15,664 samples) as if each sample were an independent observation, ignoring repeated measures within people, and adherence is pooled in the same way over 119,680 pills; the two stages of Trivedi et al. (2021) are entered as separate studies although the 225 stage-2 participants were already in stage 1. Both are unit-of-analysis errors that make intervals too narrow; heterogeneity of 89% to 99% is pooled without a prediction interval.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses excluding trials at high risk of bias are reported for use (RR 0.87) and adherence (RR 0.89) (3.4.1, 3.4.3).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Risk of bias and the very low GRADE ratings are carried into the Abstract, Discussion and Conclusion, which call the evidence low quality and the effect small.
I² is reported for every outcome, subgroup analyses explore it and the Discussion says they explain only part of it (Discussion, 10th paragraph).

Funnel plots for outcomes with five or more reports, with asymmetry recorded for each outcome in Table 3 and carried into GRADE; with five to eight reports and visual inspection only, the investigation has little power, and its likely impact is discussed only for adherence and depression.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, sponsor role and each author's competing interests are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional, because item 7 can only be judged from Appendix 5, which was not read; but no answer to item 7 could raise the rating. Two critical items are not met. The search (item 4) is wide but limits reports to seven languages without a stated reason, and AMSTAR 2 gives partial yes only when publication restrictions are justified. The statistical methods (item 11) fail because the main urine outcome and the adherence outcome treat repeated measurements within people (urine samples, pills) as independent observations, and the re-randomized stage of the combination trial is entered as a separate study, so the intervals and P values for use are too optimistic. Two critical flaws give critically low confidence. The other critical items are met or partly met: the review is registered, selected and extracted in duplicate, appraised trials with RoB 2 and graded every outcome. It can be cited for the direction of the pooled urine result, for no difference in retention, for lower adherence on bupropion and for the frequency of adverse events; it should not be cited for a precise or statistically secure effect of bupropion on use, for bupropion alone apart from the naltrexone combination, or for abstinence.

key_findings.finding: Eight placebo-controlled trials, counted by the review as 1239 participants: 611 in seven trials of bupropion alone (300 mg daily) and 628 in the two stages of Trivedi et al. (2021, bupropion 450 mg daily with naltrexone), entered as two reports; stage 2 consisted of stage-1 placebo non-responders who were re-randomized.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Results (p. 1); 3.2 Characteristics of included studies, 1st paragraph (begins p. 3); Table 1 and footnotes d and e (p. 5)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the 225 stage-2 participants were already among the 403 in stage 1, so the trials enrolled about 1014 distinct people (611 + 403), not 1239.

key_findings.finding: Main outcome, amphetamine-positive urine samples (7 reports, 15,664 samples or weeks): RR 0.90 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.96), P < .001, I² 89%; risk of bias low in 3, some concerns in 3, high in 1; minor funnel-plot asymmetry; GRADE very low. Excluding the trial at high risk of bias: 0.87 (0.83 to 0.92); excluding Elkashef et al. (2008), which reported positive weeks: 0.91 (0.85 to 0.97).
key_findings.locator: 3.4.1 Amphetamine-type stimulant use by UA, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Table 3, row ATS use by urinalysis (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The unit of analysis is the urine sample, not the person (see reporting issues), so the interval is too narrow.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups of the urine outcome: bupropion 300 mg without naltrexone (Das 2010, Elkashef 2008, Heinzerling 2013, Heinzerling 2014, Shoptaw 2008) RR 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00); 450 mg with naltrexone (the two stages of Trivedi 2021) 0.92 (0.89 to 0.94), difference not significant. Four 12-week trials 0.85 (0.78 to 0.93) vs shorter trials (Trivedi's two stages and Heinzerling 2013) 0.98 (0.89 to 1.08), a significant difference; two trials of less-than-daily use 1.09 (0.56 to 2.11); men-only (Das 2010) 0.80 (0.71 to 0.90).
key_findings.locator: 3.4.1, 2nd paragraph (p. 4); Table 4, column ATS use by UA, and its footnotes 1 to 10 (p. 9)
key_findings.note: Editors' sum from Table 1: the five bupropion-alone trials in the urine outcome enrolled 357 participants (73 + 151 + 30 + 19 + 84). Table 4 marks the bupropion-alone estimate, 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00), as individually significant (P < 0.05), so the review counts it as a reduction; at the printed precision its interval reaches 1, and with urine samples as the unit a person-level interval would be wider.

key_findings.finding: The urine outcome pools, for each arm, the overall proportion of positive urine samples (or positive weeks); samples were collected weekly in one trial, twice weekly in two and three times weekly in three. Urine results of Anderson et al. (2015; 204 participants) and Ghoreishi et al. (2017; 50) were unavailable after the authors were contacted.
key_findings.locator: 2.4 Outcome measures, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); 3.3 Selected outcomes, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Table 1 (p. 5); Table 2, column ATS use, cells for Anderson 2015 and Ghoreishi 2017 coloured as unavailable (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Retention (7 reports, 786 participants): RR 0.97 (0.89 to 1.05), I² 6%, GRADE high. Adherence by pill count (6 reports, 119,680 pills): RR 0.91 (0.84 to 0.99), favouring placebo, I² 99%, major funnel-plot asymmetry, GRADE very low; 0.89 (0.81 to 0.98) without trials at high risk of bias.
key_findings.locator: 3.4.2 Retention in treatment (begins p. 4); 3.4.3 Treatment adherence (p. 6); Table 3 (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The retention pool has seven of the eight reports with retention data; stage 1 of Trivedi et al. (2021) appears to have been left out (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Craving: at week 4 (4 reports, 373 participants) SMD 0.04 (−0.16 to 0.24), I² 0%, GRADE moderate; at the end of treatment (6 reports, 939) SMD −0.38 (−0.63 to −0.13), I² 64%, all six at high risk of bias, GRADE very low; in the one men-only trial −1.26 (−1.87 to −0.65).
key_findings.note: For Trivedi et al. (2021) the end-of-treatment craving and depression scores were built by adding the reported change to the baseline score and using the baseline SD (3.3, p. 4; Table 2 footnote, p. 6).

key_findings.finding: Depressive symptoms (5 reports, 874): SMD −0.06 (−0.26 to 0.14), I² 44%. Addiction Severity Index (2 reports, 148): legal status SMD −0.47 (−0.83 to −0.11), six other sub-scores not significant. Dropout after adverse events (4 reports, 391): RD 0.03 (−0.01 to 0.07). Serious adverse events (8 reports, 1189): RD −0.01 (−0.02 to 0.01), GRADE low.

Methods: search to 31 October 2022 in seven databases, six trial registries and grey literature; PROSPERO registration on 7 October 2022; screening, extraction, RoB 2 and GRADE in duplicate; random-effects inverse-variance pooling in Review Manager 5.4.1; funnel plots for outcomes with five or more studies; reports limited to seven languages.

The authors contrast their result with Bhatt et al. (2016), who found no effect of bupropion on sustained abstinence, noting that Bhatt et al. analysed different outcomes and did not include Trivedi et al. (2021); they add that the large Trivedi trial may have pulled the results towards benefit, although its estimate did not differ significantly from the other trials in subgroup analyses.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 8) and 10th paragraph (p. 10); 4.1 Strengths and limitations (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: bupropion may have modest benefits for amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, the clinical relevance of such a small effect should be verified, and the overall quality of evidence is low.

reporting_issues.issue: The review's total of 1239 participants adds the 403 participants of stage 1 and the 225 of stage 2 of Trivedi et al. (2021), but the stage-2 participants were stage-1 placebo non-responders who were re-randomized (3.2; Table 1 footnote e), so 225 people are counted twice; editors' calculation: the trials enrolled about 1014 distinct people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base is overstated by about a fifth, and the two stages are not independent samples; entering both as separate studies is a unit-of-analysis error.

reporting_issues.issue: The main outcome is analysed with urine samples as the unit: per-arm counts of positive samples among 15,664 samples are pooled as risk ratios as if each sample were an independent event (2.4; 2.7.1; 3.4.1; Table 3). Repeated samples from the same person are correlated. Adherence is pooled the same way over 119,680 pills. The review does not state its unit of analysis, but Table 3 gives N as samples and pills, and Table 4 gives the 30-participant men-only trial (Das et al., 2010) a urine interval of 0.80 (0.71 to 0.90), narrower than a yes-or-no outcome in 30 people could produce (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The confidence intervals and P values of every urine and adherence estimate (overall, sensitivity and subgroup) are too narrow; the statistical significance of RR 0.90 (0.84 to 0.96), and of 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00) for bupropion alone, cannot be taken at face value. The editors cannot recompute them without participant-level data.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 shows that adding Heinzerling et al. (2013), a 19-person adolescent pilot, moves two pooled estimates noticeably: the 12-week bupropion-alone trials give 0.85 (0.78 to 0.93) and all five bupropion-alone trials 0.90 (0.81 to 1.00); Trivedi's two stages give 0.92 (0.89 to 0.94) and the shorter-trials subgroup, which adds Heinzerling et al. (2013), 0.98 (0.89 to 1.08).
reporting_issues.consequence: A pilot this small can carry such weight only if its many urine samples are counted as independent observations under high heterogeneity; the subgroup estimates, including the duration finding in the Abstract, are fragile. The forest plots (Appendix 9) were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: RoB 2 is cited with Higgins et al. (2011), which describes the original Cochrane risk-of-bias tool; the judgments in Table 3 use RoB 2's words. Table 3 also rates the dropout outcome 'Medium', which is not a GRADE level, and the text cites the GRADE table once as Appendix 8 and elsewhere as Appendix 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation and labelling errors; the dropout rating is presumably moderate.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks retention as available for eight reports, including both stages of Trivedi et al. (2021), but the pooled retention analysis has seven reports and 786 participants (3.4.2, p. 4; Table 3, p. 7), and Table 4 lists one 450-mg report. The eight reports enrolled 1189 people by Table 1 (p. 5); 786 is that total less the 403 of stage 1 (editors' calculation), so stage 1 appears to have been left out without comment.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the retention estimate (0.97, 0.89 to 1.05) probably omits the larger stage of the combination trial, which avoids counting stage-2 participants twice in this outcome, but the choice is not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that Trivedi et al. combined 450 mg bupropion with naloxone (p. 10); the trial used extended-release injectable naltrexone (Table 1 footnote c, p. 5; Introduction, p. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error with no consequence for the results.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 4 the urine subgroup with mixed use frequency is printed with N = 5, but its footnote 3 lists three trials (Das et al., 2010; Elkashef et al., 2008; Shoptaw et al., 2008); the other two reports are presumably the two stages of Trivedi et al. (2021), the only urine reports not in the less-than-daily subgroup (footnote 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling omission; the subgroup composition can be inferred.

disagreements.first_pass: risk_of_bias.domains[3].judgment: partial-yes; risk_of_bias.domains[3].note: but reports were limited to seven languages without a stated reason.; risk_of_bias.overall: low-confidence; risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: item 7 can only be judged from Appendix 5, which was not read. One critical item fails: the main urine outcome and the adherence outcome treat repeated measurements within people (urine samples, pills) as independent observations, and the re-randomized stage of the combination trial is entered as a separate study, so the intervals and P values for use are too optimistic; that alone gives low confidence, and critically low if item 7 were also not met. The other critical items are met or partly met: the review is registered, searched widely, selected and extracted in duplicate, appraised trials with RoB 2 and graded every outcome. It can be cited for the direction of the pooled urine result, for no difference in retention, for lower adherence on bupropion and for the frequency of adverse events; it should not be cited for a precise or statistically secure effect of bupropion on use, for bupropion alone apart from the naltrexone combination, or for abstinence.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 17: disagree on item 4 and the overall: item 4 (critical) should be no, not partial yes, because partial yes requires justified publication restrictions and reports were limited to seven languages (2.3, p. 2) with no justification; with item 11 also not met there are two critical flaws, so the overall is critically low confidence, provisional while item 7 rests on the unread Appendix 5. Agrees with every other item. Under the lenient reading the card's low confidence (provisional) would stand.
disagreements.resolution: Applied AMSTAR 2 item 4 as written, as the adjudication brief directs for every card in this batch: the language limit (2.3, p. 2) has no stated reason, so partial yes is not available. With item 11 also not met, two critical items fail, which gives critically low confidence whatever item 7 shows; the rating stays marked provisional because item 7 rests on the unread Appendix 5. The first reader's overall (low) followed from the lenient reading of item 4; the readers agree on every other item, so no disagreement on the overall remains.
